summary: Planet X · SPHEREx Observation Lab is a public web tool that shows how the infrared sky changes over time and where the search for a ninth planet stands. It connects three things in one interface. First, real SPHEREx Level-2 images from NASA/IPAC IRSA: for the five official test targets (Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae, R Draconis), Pluto and the four giant planets, users compare two epochs side by side or as a blink animation, with the mission's quality flags, wavelength and observation time. Second, a 3D Solar System out to 1,000 AU built from NASA/JPL Horizons ephemerides and 8,341 trans-Neptunian objects from the JPL Small-Body Database. Third, the published Planet Nine reference population of 100,000 orbits: a user picks one hypothesis, sees its predicted sky path, and asks the IRSA MOST service which SPHEREx exposures covered that position. Every image keeps its source URL and SHA-256 hash, and every judgement can be saved, exported and restored. We label observation, calculation and hypothesis separately and claim no detection. The site works in five languages, so students and the public, not only specialists, can explore NASA's newest all-sky survey.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Planet X · SPHEREx Observation Lab (https://nasaspaceappschallenge.marulee.dev/) has three linked workspaces.

1. Explore. A 3D Solar System from the Sun to 1,000 AU: 476 Solar System bodies (planets, dwarf planets and natural satellites) with NASA/JPL data, plus 8,341 trans-Neptunian objects (TNOs) from the JPL Small-Body Database drawn as a GPU point cloud. Users search or click any body to see its orbit, its measured or estimated mass, and whether it meets the three IAU planet criteria. A time control replays positions from 3000 BCE to 3000 CE.

2. Actual observations. Real SPHEREx Level-2 spectral images (QR2, QR3 and DR1) for 10 targets: the five official challenge test targets (Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae, R Draconis), Pluto, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. 40 image products form 37 same-detector pairs taken at different times, with baselines of up to 17 months. Users view a pair side by side or as a blink animation, change the contrast, hover to read native pixel values (MJy/sr), and read a quality panel built from the mission's own FLAGS, VARIANCE and ZODI layers before making a judgement.

3. Planet Nine hypothesis. We load the published reference population of 100,000 synthetic Planet Nine orbits (Brown & Batygin 2021). After removing orbits that the ZTF, DES and Pan-STARRS1 surveys would already have detected, 20,406 remain within 1,000 AU. The tool ranks HEALPix sky cells by how many of these orbits fall in them, lets the user pick one orbit as a hypothesis, computes its sky path with light-time correction, compares it with real TNO orbits, and queries NASA/IPAC IRSA's Moving Object Search Tool (MOST) to list the SPHEREx exposures that covered the predicted position.

Evidence. In both the observation and the hypothesis workspace the user can write a judgement, save it, export it as JSON or CSV and restore it later. The record keeps observation IDs, times, source URLs and SHA-256 hashes.

HOW IT ADDRESSES THE CHALLENGE

The challenge asks for a public-facing web tool that displays SPHEREx images and makes changes over time easy to see, tested on five named targets. All five are included with real multi-epoch SPHEREx data and a blink animation. From the optional considerations we implemented: metadata display including contamination flags; data from several detector arrays (D1, D3, D6) with the wavelength of each exposure; a manifest-driven observation registry so that new SPHEREx releases can be added without changing the interface (DR1 images were added within days of their release); and Astropy for all FITS handling.

WHY IT MATTERS

Neptune was predicted by calculation in 1846 before anyone saw it. Planet Nine is a similar prediction today. A planet of 5 to 10 Earth masses would test planetary migration theory, explain the clustered orbits of distant Kuiper Belt objects, and give us a nearby example of a type of planet that is common around other stars but missing from our Solar System. Earlier surveys have ruled out about 78% of its predicted positions (Brown, Holman & Batygin 2024). Our tool shows the public where the remaining search area is, what a real all-sky infrared survey has imaged there, and how to judge such data critically.

HOW IT WORKS

- Build pipeline (Python 3.12, Astropy, NumPy): downloads original SPHEREx FITS files (about 66 MB each) from IRSA, checks SHA-256 hashes, cuts native-pixel cutouts around the predicted target position, reads the FLAGS, VARIANCE and ZODI planes and the spectral WCS, and writes a verified cache. Target positions come from JPL Horizons observer ephemerides for the SPHEREx spacecraft (Solar System bodies) and from SIMBAD proper motions (Epsilon Indi B).

- Server (Node.js 22, built-in HTTP and worker threads, no external runtime packages): serves the API (OpenAPI contract), verifies source hashes, runs orbit prediction and the live MOST query, and stores evidence files.

- Front end (TypeScript, React, Vite, Three.js/WebGL, i18next): 3D scene, comparison viewer and evidence panels in English, Korean, Japanese, Traditional Chinese and French.

- Hosting: AWS EC2 (m7i.xlarge, Ubuntu 24.04), nginx, HTTPS.

- Testing: Node and Python unit tests, Vitest, TypeScript strict mode, Ruff, and browser checks in Chrome. Interpolated planet positions were compared with 27 separate JPL Horizons queries; the largest difference was about 19 km.

HOW WE TESTED

All requests, bugs and science questions went into one shared tracker that every team member could write to. It holds 41 numbered entries (R001 to R041), each with its author, type, location and status (completed, on hold or rejected).

- Specification and science checks (12 entries, planning stage on 13 November): our science reviewer recomputed the planning values by hand, for example Pluto's predicted shift between 29 September and 2 October (72.3 arcsec, about 11.8 SPHEREx pixels at 6.15 arcsec per pixel), Epsilon Indi B's proper motion over 511.6 days (6.56 arcsec, about 1.07 pixels), and the conversion 1 MJy/sr = 0.889 mJy per pixel.

- Bugs and usability (29 entries, during the event): testers reported broken planet textures after selection, inconsistent zoom distances, empty comparison panels for targets without linked exposures, side panels that could not be reopened, evidence JSON that did not restore, and a broken layout on phones. Most were fixed during the event; phones now get a clear notice instead of a broken page.

- Scope: a tracker entry on day two led us to remove the galaxy map, cosmic history, comet and physics-lab features and to refocus on Planet Nine. Two feature requests (habitable zone, a quasar) were rejected as off-topic.

WHAT IS CREATIVE

- It connects a hypothesis to a prediction, the prediction to real telescope coverage, and the result to a saved evidence record, in one flow.

- It treats scientific honesty as a design feature: every screen states whether a value is observed, calculated or hypothetical, and quality flags are shown before any conclusion.

- 8,341 real TNO orbits can be compared with any chosen Planet Nine orbit by semi-major axis, eccentricity and inclination.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Accuracy over spectacle: sizes and distances in the 3D scene are labelled as compressed, and unknown masses stay unknown. Because SPHEREx samples a different wavelength in each exposure, a brightness change alone is not treated as variability.

- Data rights: every source keeps its credit and terms, no NASA logos are used, and no AI-generated image replaces an observation.

- Performance: heavy FITS processing is done ahead of time so the site stays responsive.

- Privacy: the site shows only approved nicknames and stores no personal data.

- Scope: during the hackathon we removed galaxy, exoplanet and cosmology features to focus on the Solar System within 1,000 AU and on the challenge itself.

LIMITS AND NEXT STEPS

- Images are native cutouts centred on each predicted position and are not yet registered to each other, so the tool does not measure motion or brightness. Spectral calibration is unverified for 23 of the 40 products, and the interface says so.

- A coverage match from MOST means that an exposure contains the predicted position. It is not a detection.

- Next: search by RA/Dec and by URL for any sky position with on-demand cutouts; image registration and difference images; overlays from Gaia DR3 and WISE; CSA NEOSSat data; sensitivity tests with injected sources; mobile support.
